body:
- **Value and Momentum Everywhere** (Asness, Moskowitz, Pedersen, *Journal of Finance* 2013): value and momentum premia appear in 8 markets/asset classes (US, UK, Europe and Japan stocks; index futures; bonds; FX; commodities). Value and momentum are negatively correlated with each other, so combining them diversifies. Global funding-liquidity risk is a partial driver. — [AQR](https://www.aqr.com/Insights/Research/Journal-Article/Value-and-Momentum-Everywhere); [NYU PDF](https://pages.stern.nyu.edu/~lpederse/papers/ValMomEverywhere.pdf)
- **Quality Minus Junk** (Asness, Frazzini, Pedersen, *Review of Accounting Studies* 2019): going long profitable, growing, safe stocks (low leverage, stable profitability, low credit risk) and short junk earns significant risk-adjusted returns. When quality is expensive, it predicts lower future relative returns. Returns are gross of costs. — [SSRN](https://papers.ssrn.com/abstract=2312432); [CBS PDF](https://research-api.cbs.dk/ws/portalfiles/portal/60211462/lasse_heje_pedersen_et_al_quality_minus_junk_publishersversion.pdf); [CXO Advisory critique](https://www.cxoadvisory.com/?p=23772)
- **Betting Against Beta** (Frazzini and Pedersen, *JFE* 2013): long low-beta (levered to beta 1), short high-beta. It is driven by leverage constraints and loses money when credit constraints tighten. It works within and across industries. — [NBER PDF](https://conference.nber.org/confer/2010/BEf10/Frazzini.pdf); [AQR FAJ](https://www.Aqr.Com/-/media/AQR/Documents/Insights/Journal-Article/FAJ-LowRisk-Investing-Without-Industry-Bets.pdf)
- "Size matters if you control your junk": the small-cap premium reappears once you exclude junk. — [Wharton PDF](https://jacobslevycenter.wharton.upenn.edu/wp-content/uploads/2015/05/Size-Matters-if-You-Control-Your-Junk.pdf)
- **Renaissance Medallion**: Bradford Cornell calculated average annual returns of about 66% gross (after trading costs, before fees) and about 39% net, 1988–2018. He found no "convincing" explanation. Zuckerman cites "ample and cheap leverage." Medallion is closed to outsiders, and RenTec's outside funds are "relatively mundane." A 2024 paper argues these averages should not be labelled CAGRs. — [Institutional Investor](https://www.institutionalinvestor.com/article/b1k2fymby99nj0/Famed-Medallion-Fund-Stretches-Explanation-to-the-Limit-Professor-Claims); [PWL Capital](https://pwlcapital.com/renaissance-technologies-medallion-fund-an-exception-to-the-indexing-rule/); [Institutional Investor, Medallion vs other RenTec funds](https://inv.institutionalinvestor.com/index%2ephp/article/2bswzoz7x91fqht87wvsw/portfolio/the-famed-medallion-fund-is-crushing-it-other-rentech-funds-not-so-much)

body:
**Early capital and work ethic (pre-1956)**
- Delivered newspapers, sold refurbished golf balls and stamp sets, and ran pinball machines in barbershops. From all his ventures combined he had saved about **$9,800** by around the time he finished school [SECONDARY]. I found no source confirming the exact age or the "Washington Post route" detail — [Frederik Journals, "The Hustler"](https://www.frederikjournals.com/p/the-hustler-lessons-from-a-young); [Saber Capital, Buffett's Early Investments](https://sabercapitalmgt.com/buffetts-early-investments/)
- **Moody's manuals:** Buffett reportedly went through about 20,000 pages of the Moody's industrial, transportation, bank and finance manuals, twice. In early 1952, while flipping through the Moody's Bank & Finance manual at his Omaha brokerage job, he found **Western Insurance Securities**. He recalled its "price range in Moody's financial manual was $12 to $20" while it earned about $24/share the prior year, so it traded at roughly 1x earnings [SECONDARY] — [findvalue23, Western Insurance](https://findvalue23.substack.com/p/history-warren-buffett-and-western); [GuruFocus, Western Insurance](https://www.gurufocus.com/news/1149512/some-thoughts-on-warren-buffetts-early-investments-in-western-insurance-services)
- **GEICO 1951:** about 65% of his net worth (about $10,282) went into GEICO in 1951. He sold in 1952 for $15,259 and rotated into cheaper stocks such as Western Insurance [SECONDARY]. He later called selling GEICO a costly error — [GuruFocus "How Buffett Crushed the Dow in 1951"](https://www.gurufocus.com/news/248721/how-buffett-crushed-the-dow-in-1951-lessons-for-investing-with-small-sums); [Fool](https://www.fool.com/investing/2019/12/29/heres-how-much-money-warren-buffett-has-made-in-ge.aspx)
- **1951 personal return:** about **75.8% vs. the Dow's 21.3%** [SECONDARY]. A circulating "144%" figure for 1951 has no source I could find [MYTH/DISPUTED] — [GuruFocus](https://www.gurufocus.com/news/248721/how-buffett-crushed-the-dow-in-1951-lessons-for-investing-with-small-sums)
- **Graham-Newman apprenticeship, 1954–56:** starting salary **$12,000/yr**. The sources agree on these dates; one outlier says 1951 [SECONDARY] — [Financial History magazine](https://fhmagazine.org/financial-history-134-summer-2020/0850549001596540706/p15); [dividendgrowthinvestor](https://dividendgrowthinvestor.com/2020/08/warren-buffett-americas-youngest-early.html)

`person:group-piramal` · flag: **mostly-clean** · confidence: verified · tickers: PIRAMALFIN, PPLPHARMA

Flag: MOSTLY-CLEAN (governance) with an aggressive deal/capital-allocation record. Ajay Piramal is a serial asset trader: sold the domestic formulations business to Abbott (2010, ~$3.7bn), traded a Vodafone India stake (2011-14), took and exited a Shriram group stake, then pivoted Piramal Enterprises (PEL) into real-estate wholesale lending (2014-2019) -- a concentrated book that hurt after IL&FS (2018-19). PEL acquired DHFL via IBC (2021, ~Rs 34,250 cr plan), giving a large retail book plus legacy recoveries. Structure changes: pharma vertically demerged into Piramal Pharma (2022; 4 PPL shares per PEL share); PEL merged into wholly owned Piramal Finance effective 16-Sep-2025 (1:1 swap; PEL delisted, Piramal Finance listed), with Anand Piramal as chair. No promoter pledging; no SEBI/ED findings against promoters found. Points to watch: frequent restructurings (each one resets comparables), legacy wholesale write-downs, alternate-investment-fund (AIF) structures flagged by RBI in 2023 (evergreening rules), and promoter-group real-estate (Piramal Realty, unlisted) interactions with the lender. Good conduct: demergers gave mirror shareholding; buybacks/dividends from PEL historically; rights issues offered to all. Status Nov-2026: Piramal Finance is the listed lending entity; no open governance actions found.

- **red flags:** concentrated wholesale RE lending; frequent restructurings; AIF exposure (RBI 2023)
- **good conduct:** mirror demergers; no pledges

- **id:** `thesis:paper-call:US-TGT:q4-2026-comps-3pct-plus`
- **Method:** base rate · **P(ours)** 0.62 · **P(base)** 0.55 · resolve by 2027-03-15
- **Evidence:** 8-K 18-Nov-2026 (Q3 2026): net sales +7.1%, comparable sales +5.6% (traffic +5.0%; stores +4.6%, digital +9.8%); November month-to-date 'in line with the Company's guidance… accelerating from October'. FY2026 guide raised: net sales growth ~6% (+1 pt), operating margin ~6.2% incl. ~1.1 pt tariff-refund benefit, EPS $10.65–11.40. Q4 2025 is an easy compare (Target's comps were negative through 2025).
- **Why our number differs from base:** Traffic-led comps and an easy compare favour ≥3%; risks are a weaker holiday consumer (rate hikes, inflation) and the 53rd/calendar shift noise.
- **Base-rate reasoning:** A retailer comping +5–6% with traffic leading sustains ≥3% the next quarter roughly 55% of the time.
- **Resolution rule:** YES if Target's reported Q4 2026 comparable sales change (Q4 earnings release) ≥ +3.0%.
- **Resolution source:** Target Q4 2026 earnings 8-K (SEC EDGAR, CIK 27419)
- **Sources used:** https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/27419/000002741926000051/a2026q3ex-99.htm

- **id:** `thesis:paper-call:BAJAJCON:fy27-revenue-growth-17pct-plus`
- **Method:** promise-tracker credibility · **P(ours)** 0.52 · **P(base)** 0.55 · resolve by 2027-05-31
- **Evidence:** Q2 FY27 call (15-Oct-2026): H1 revenue ₹674 cr (+28%), H1 EBITDA ₹167 cr (+85%), Q2 EBITDA margin 25%; Almond Drops double-digit unit volume growth; GT and organized trade both 'mid-20s' growth. MD Naveen Pandey: 'for the year, we are expecting a high teens' growth. Gross margin 59.9% (West Asia war, edible-oil inflation); ~5% consumer price increase in Q3 (2–3% frontal + ml-age cut). Screener: FY26 sales ₹1,165 cr; quarterly sales Q3 FY26 306 (+31%), Q4 FY26 327 (+30%), Q1 FY27 342, Q2 FY27 333.
- **Why our number differs from base:** H1 at +28% makes a high-teens year look easy, but the H2 base is hard (H2 FY26 grew ~30%), so ≥17% needs H2 growth of ~+10% while the company takes price and cuts ml-age into an inflationary rural market. Management's own 'high teens' (not 'mid-20s') signals they expect H2 to slow sharply. We sit fractionally below base.
- **Base-rate reasoning:** Small-cap FMCG companies restating a full-year growth range at H1 with H1 well above it meet the range's lower part roughly 55% of the time when the H2 comparison base is much tougher.
- **Resolution rule:** YES if Bajaj Consumer Care's FY27 consolidated revenue from operations ÷ FY26 consolidated revenue from operations − 1 ≥ 17.0% (company's own reported growth figure if stated; else from the audited results; screener.in annual table as fallback).
- **Resolution source:** Bajaj Consumer Care Q4 FY27 results / investor presentation (NSE); screener.in
- **Sources used:** https://nsearchives.nseindia.in/corporate/BAJAJCON_21102026110839_Exchanges_Transcript.pdf; https://www.screener.in/company/BAJAJCON/consolidated/
- **Confidence of evidence:** verified
